title: Conjunctions and Connectives
summary: Coordinating and subordinating conjunctions, connectives grouped by function (time, cause, contrast, addition and more), how to link paragraphs, and how Checkpoint 6 asks about them.

blocks.text: 1. What are conjunctions and connectives?

Writers need words that **join ideas** and show **how the ideas are connected**. Without them, writing sounds like a list of separate facts. With them, the reader understands the order of events, the reasons, the results and the differences.

rows: **Conjunction**
joins words or clauses **inside one sentence**
I was hungry, **so** I made a sandwich. / I stayed home **because** I was ill.
**Connective** (also called a linking word or adverbial)
links one sentence to another, or one paragraph to the next
The plan was simple. **However**, nothing went as planned.

blocks.text: In Checkpoint 6, connectives matter in **both sections** of both papers:

items: **Reading:** you may be asked what a joining word shows (time, reason, contrast...), or **how the start of a paragraph links to the paragraph before it**.

**Writing:** linking ideas and paragraphs clearly helps your mark for **Structure of texts (7 marks)**, and joining clauses correctly helps **Grammar and punctuation (7 marks)**. Choosing a precise connective also shows good **Vocabulary and language**.

blocks.title: Exam words
items: **Function**: the job a word does (adds, contrasts, gives a reason, shows time...).
**Cohesion**: how well the parts of a text stick together and flow.
**Link back**: when the start of a paragraph refers to an idea in the paragraph before.
**Sequence**: the order in which things happen.

blocks.text: 2. Coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS)
Coordinating conjunctions join two words, two phrases or two **main clauses** of **equal** importance. There are seven: **F**or, **A**nd, **N**or, **B**ut, **O**r, **Y**et, **S**o.

rows: for
reason (like *because*, but formal and old-fashioned)
The traveller rested, for he had walked all day.
and
addition: adds one idea to another
The sun came out, and the birds began to sing.
nor
adds a second **negative** idea
She did not cry, nor did she complain.
but
contrast: shows a difference
The cake looked delicious, but it tasted terrible.
or
choice: gives an alternative
You can have juice or water.
yet
contrast: something surprising
He practised every day, yet he still felt nervous.
so
result: shows what happened because of something
The river flooded, so the road was closed.

blocks.text: 3. Subordinating conjunctions
Subordinating conjunctions start a **subordinate clause** and join it to a **main clause**. They show exactly how the two ideas are related. Learn them by **function**:

rows: Time
when, while, as, before, after, until, since, once, whenever
**Before** you leave, switch off the lights.
Cause / reason
because, since, as
We cancelled the picnic **because** it was raining.
Contrast
although, though, even though, while, whereas
**Although** the test was hard, everyone finished.
Condition
if, unless, as long as, provided that
You can play **as long as** you finish your homework.
Purpose
so that, in order that
He saved his money **so that** he could buy a bike.
Place
where, wherever
Plant the seeds **where** they will get sunlight.
Comparison
than, as ... as
Our team ran faster **than** we expected.
Choice / doubt
whether
I don't know **whether** the shop is open.

blocks.title: Same word, different jobs
items: **since**: time (*I have lived here since 2020.*) or reason (*Since you are here, let's start.*)
**as**: time (*As I opened the door, the phone rang.*) or reason (*As it was late, we took a taxi.*)
**while**: time (*While I cooked, he set the table.*) or contrast (*Ali loves maths, while his brother prefers art.*)
Always read the whole sentence to decide the function.

blocks.text: 4. Pairs that work together
Some conjunctions come in **pairs** (they are called correlative conjunctions). Use both parts.

rows: both ... and
adds two things together
**Both** the teacher **and** the students enjoyed the trip.
either ... or
a choice between two
You can **either** walk **or** take the bus.
neither ... nor
two negatives (not this and not that)
**Neither** the cat **nor** the dog wanted to go outside.
not only ... but also
adds with emphasis
She is **not only** clever **but also** very kind.
whether ... or
two possibilities
**Whether** you like it **or** not, the exam is on Monday.

blocks.text: 5. Connectives that link sentences and paragraphs

These words and phrases usually come at the **start** of a sentence or paragraph, followed by a comma (*However, ... / In addition, ...*). They are the key to well-linked writing. Learn them in groups by function:

rows: Addition (adding more)
Also, In addition, Furthermore, Moreover, What is more, Besides
Walking is good for your heart. **In addition**, it costs nothing.
Contrast (showing a difference)
However, On the other hand, Nevertheless, Even so, In contrast, Instead
Many people like the new park. **However**, some say it is too noisy.
Cause and result
Therefore, As a result, Consequently, Because of this, For this reason, That is why
The bridge was damaged. **As a result**, the road was closed for a week.
Time and sequence
First, Firstly, Next, Then, After that, Later, Meanwhile, Soon, Finally, Eventually, At last
**First**, wash the rice. **Next**, add the water.
Example
For example, For instance, One example is
Some animals sleep all winter. **For example**, bears hibernate for months.
Emphasis
Indeed, In fact, Above all, Most importantly, Clearly
**Above all**, never swim alone.
Similarity
Similarly, Likewise, In the same way
Cats need exercise. **Similarly**, dogs need a daily walk.
Condition
Otherwise, If so, In that case
Bring a coat. **Otherwise**, you will be cold.
Summing up / ending
In conclusion, To sum up, Overall, All in all, Finally
**Overall**, the trip was a great success.

blocks.text: 6. Linking paragraphs: how good writers do it

The examiner wants your paragraphs to **flow** from one to the next. Here are five ways to link the start of a paragraph to the one before. Reading questions sometimes ask **how the start of a paragraph links to the previous paragraph**, so learn to spot these too.

rows: 1. A time connective
*Later that afternoon, the storm finally reached the village.*
moves the story forward in time from the last paragraph
2. A contrast connective
*However, not everyone agrees with this idea.*
turns from one side of an argument to the other
3. An addition connective
*Another reason to visit the museum is its café.*
adds a new point to the reasons already given
4. A word that points back (this, these, that, such)
*This discovery changed everything.*
*This* refers to the discovery described in the last paragraph
5. Repeating or echoing a key word
Last paragraph ends: *...a strange light in the window.* Next starts: *The light grew brighter.*
picks up the same idea so the reader follows the thread

blocks.text: **Worked example.** Read these two original paragraphs:
*Paragraph 1:* Every summer, thousands of turtles come to the beaches of the Red Sea to lay their eggs. They dig deep holes in the sand at night and bury the eggs carefully.
*Paragraph 2:* **Sadly, these nests are often in danger.** Bright lights from hotels confuse the baby turtles, and people walking on the beach can crush the eggs.
**Question:** How does the first sentence of paragraph 2 link to paragraph 1? (1 mark)
**Answer:** It uses *these nests* to point back to the holes and eggs described in paragraph 1, and *Sadly* shows a change from the turtles' careful work to the dangers they face.

blocks.title: Paragraph link answer frame
blocks.text: Quote the linking word or phrase → say what it **refers back to** in the previous paragraph → say what it **does** (moves on in time / adds a new point / introduces the other side / introduces a problem).
7. Which connectives suit which text?

rows: Story
Paper 2
time connectives to move the plot: *Suddenly, Moments later, Meanwhile, That night, Eventually, At last*
Recount, diary, biography, news report
Paper 1
time and sequence: *First, Later, After that, The next morning, By the evening, Finally*
Instructions
Paper 1
sequence: *First, Next, Then, After that, Finally*, and also *When ... , Once ... , Before ...*
Persuasive writing (letter, leaflet, advert, speech)
Paper 1
addition and emphasis: *Furthermore, What is more, Above all, Clearly* / cause: *Therefore, As a result*
Balanced argument / discussion
Paper 1
contrast: *However, On the other hand, In contrast* / ending: *Overall, To sum up, In conclusion*
Information text / non-chronological report
Paper 1
addition and example: *Also, In addition, For example, Similarly*
Review
Paper 1
contrast and summing up: *However, Although, Overall*

blocks.text: 8. Common mistakes with connectives

rows: Using two contrast words together
*Although it was cold, but we went out.*
*Although it was cold, we went out.* / *It was cold, but we went out.*
A *because* clause left alone
*We stayed inside. Because it was raining.*
*We stayed inside because it was raining.*
Using the wrong function
*The shop was closed. Furthermore, we went home.*
*The shop was closed. As a result, we went home.* (it is a result, not an addition)
Repeating the same connective
*And then... and then... and then...*
Change it: *After that... Later... Finally...*
*However* used like *but* in the middle with only a comma
*I wanted to go, however I was too tired.*
*I wanted to go. However, I was too tired.* / *I wanted to go, but I was too tired.*
*So* at the start of every sentence in formal writing
*So the council should act. So the park will be safe.*
*Therefore, the council should act. As a result, the park will be safe.*

blocks.title: Too many connectives
blocks.text: Do not start **every** sentence with a connective. One at the start of each paragraph and a few inside paragraphs is enough. Too many make writing sound heavy and unnatural.
9. How Checkpoint asks about connectives
These are typical question styles, written in our own words:

rows: Which word in this sentence is a conjunction? / Circle the conjunction.
Find the word that joins two clauses: FANBOYS or a starter like *because, when, although, if*.
What does the word *however* (or *although*, *so*, *meanwhile*) show here?
Name the function: contrast, cause, result, time, addition, condition. Add a few words about what is being contrasted or caused.
Choose the best word to join these two sentences.
Read both ideas. Ask: is the second one a reason? a result? a surprise? Then pick the matching connective.
How does the start of paragraph 3 link to paragraph 2?
Quote the link (*This...*, *However...*, *Later...*), say what it refers back to, and say what it does.
Why does the writer use *Suddenly* at the start of this paragraph?
Any of these effects: it shows a quick, unexpected change / it surprises or shocks the reader / it speeds up the action / it builds suspense about what will happen next.

blocks.text: 10. Practice A: what does the connective show?

items.q: *The museum was crowded. Nevertheless, we saw every room.* What does *Nevertheless* show?
items.a: **Contrast.** Even though it was crowded (a problem), they still saw every room.

items.q: *We left early so that we could avoid the traffic.* What does *so that* show?
items.a: **Purpose.** It explains why they left early.

items.q: *You will not pass unless you revise.* What does *unless* show?
items.a: **Condition.** Passing depends on revising.

items.q: *The power went off. Consequently, the food in the fridge spoiled.* What does *Consequently* show?
items.a: **Result.** The food spoiled because the power went off.

items.q: *While Dad drove, we played games in the back.* What does *While* show here?
items.a: **Time.** The two actions happened at the same time.

items.q: *Cats are independent pets, whereas dogs need lots of attention.* What does *whereas* show?
items.a: **Contrast** between cats and dogs.

blocks.text: 11. Practice B: join the sentences
Join each pair using the type of word given in brackets.

items.q: The ice was thin. We did not skate on the lake. (result)
items.a: *The ice was thin, so we did not skate on the lake.* / *Because the ice was thin, we did not skate on the lake.*

items.q: Sami is very shy. He sang in front of the whole school. (contrast)
items.a: *Although Sami is very shy, he sang in front of the whole school.* / *Sami is very shy, yet he sang in front of the whole school.*

items.q: The baby fell asleep. We turned the music off. (time)
items.a: *When the baby fell asleep, we turned the music off.* / *After the baby fell asleep, we turned the music off.*

items.q: You can have the red bag. You can have the blue bag. (choice, pair)
items.a: *You can have either the red bag or the blue bag.*

items.q: Recycling saves energy. It reduces rubbish. (addition, pair)
items.a: *Recycling not only saves energy but also reduces rubbish.*

blocks.text: 12. Practice C: choose the best connective

items.q: Mix the flour and sugar. ______, add the eggs one at a time. (However / Next / For example)
items.a: **Next.** This is a sequence in instructions.

items.q: Some people think school uniform is boring. ______, others say it saves time every morning. (On the other hand / As a result / Finally)
items.a: **On the other hand.** It introduces the opposite view.

items.q: Exercise keeps your body healthy. ______, it can make you feel happier. (Instead / In addition / Otherwise)
items.a: **In addition.** It adds a second benefit.

items.q: Leave the gate shut. ______, the goats will escape. (Otherwise / Similarly / Meanwhile)
items.a: **Otherwise.** It shows what will happen if the condition is not met.

items.q: Ahmed searched for hours. ______, he found the key under the sofa. (At last / For instance / However)
items.a: **At last.** It shows the long wait is over.

blocks.text: 13. Practice D: linking paragraphs

items.q: Paragraph 1 describes how a family planned a picnic all week. Paragraph 2 begins: *Unfortunately, the weather had other plans.* How does this link to paragraph 1? (1 mark)
items.a: *Unfortunately* shows a contrast: after all the happy planning in paragraph 1, something goes wrong. The phrase *the weather had other plans* prepares the reader for a problem.

items.q: Paragraph 2 of an information text ends by describing how bees make honey. Paragraph 3 begins: *This honey is not only food for bees.* How does it link back?
items.a: *This honey* points back to the honey described in paragraph 2, and *not only* shows that a new point about its other uses is being added.

items.q: Write a first sentence for a new paragraph that moves a story forward in time.
items.a: Example: *By the time the sun rose, the boat was far out at sea.*

items.q: Write a first sentence for a paragraph that gives the opposite view in a balanced argument about homework.
items.a: Example: *On the other hand, some parents believe that homework takes away time for family and play.*

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Conjunctions join ideas **inside** a sentence. Connectives link **sentences and paragraphs**. Always know the **function**: addition, contrast, cause, result, time, condition, example or summing up.
